subject: Chemistry
source: AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462 specification (2016 onwards) — Y10 covered topic codes C1–C5 (Atomic structure and the periodic table; Bonding, structure and properties of matter; Quantitative chemistry; Chemical changes; Energy changes) plus Required Practicals 1–4.

specPoints.specTitle: Atoms, elements and compounds: definitions, chemical symbols and the use of word and balanced symbol equations
Mixtures: methods of separation including filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography
The atom: nucleus (protons and neutrons), electrons in shells; relative charges, masses and the radius of the atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m)
Atomic number, mass number and isotopes; calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from isotope abundances (HT only)
Electronic structure: arrangement of electrons in shells (e.g. 2,8,8); link to position in the periodic table
Development of the model of the atom: Dalton, plum-pudding, Rutherford, Bohr, discovery of neutrons
The periodic table: arranged by atomic number; Mendeleev's contribution; metals and non-metals; Group 0 noble gases
Group 1 alkali metals: properties and reactions with water; trends in reactivity down the group
Group 7 halogens: physical properties; displacement reactions; trends in reactivity down the group
Transition metals: typical properties compared with Group 1 — higher melting points, harder, denser, less reactive, form coloured compounds, used as catalysts (HT only — full comparison)
Chemical bonds — ionic, covalent, metallic; formation of ions by gain or loss of electrons; charges on simple ions
Ionic bonding: formation of ionic compounds between metals and non-metals; representation as dot-and-cross diagrams
Covalent bonding: formation of single, double and triple bonds; dot-and-cross diagrams for simple molecules (H₂, Cl₂, O₂, N₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄)
Metallic bonding: structure of giant metallic lattices; explanation of conductivity, malleability and high melting points
Properties of ionic compounds: high melting and boiling points; conduction of electricity when molten or in solution
Properties of small molecules and giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide); link structure to properties
Polymers: long-chain molecules; properties relating to chain length and intermolecular forces
Carbon allotropes: diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes (including C₆₀ buckminsterfullerene) and carbon nanotubes; uses linked to structure
Conservation of mass and balanced symbol equations; mass changes when a reactant or product is a gas; relative formula mass
Moles: Avogadro's constant (6.02 × 10²³); calculate moles from mass; calculate masses of reactants and products from balanced equations (HT only)
Limiting reactants and uncertainty (HT only — calculate using moles)
Concentration of solutions: g/dm³ and mol/dm³ (HT for mol/dm³); calculate concentration in solutions
Reactivity series of metals: reactions with water, oxygen and dilute acids; placement of carbon and hydrogen
Extraction of metals: reduction with carbon for metals less reactive than carbon; electrolysis of more reactive metals
Oxidation and reduction: defined in terms of oxygen; oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer (HT only)
Reactions of acids: with metals (acid + metal → salt + hydrogen); with metal oxides, hydroxides and carbonates; neutralisation
The pH scale and indicators; strong vs weak acids and the relationship between pH and hydrogen ion concentration (HT only — pH change of factor 10)
Required practical: preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate (e.g. copper sulfate)
Electrolysis of molten ionic compounds: positive ions to cathode, negative ions to anode; products explained
Electrolysis of aqueous solutions: prediction of products considering reactivity series; half-equations at electrodes (HT only — half-equations)
Energy changes in reactions: exothermic and endothermic reactions and their everyday uses (hand warmers, sports injury packs)
Reaction profiles: activation energy; profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions
Bond energies: calculate the overall energy change for a reaction using bond energies (HT only)
Required Practical 1: Make a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate
Required Practical 2: Determine the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration
Required Practical 3: Investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions (e.g. acid + alkali, displacement reactions)
Required Practical 4: Investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert electrodes
